DLYRPM.overview: DLYRPM defines the engine speed threshold that switches the stationary closed-throttle dashpot delay between the standard low-RPM timer DLYTIM2 and the extended high-RPM timer DLYTM3. When the accelerator pedal is released at a standstill, the severity of the deceleration depends heavily on engine speed. If the engine was merely idling or gently revved below DLYRPM, a brief dashpot delay (DLYTIM2) is sufficient to catch the engine smoothly. However, if the engine was revved to high RPM above DLYRPM, the extended dashpot delay (DLYTM3) is required to ensure safe recovery. In factory calibrations, DLYRPM is set to 94 counts, corresponding to an engine speed threshold of approximately 1504 RPM (nominally 1500 RPM).

MPHREF.overview: MPHREF defines the critical vehicle speed threshold that separates moving or rolling deceleration logic from stationary closed-throttle idle control. When a vehicle is moving down the road at highway or suburban speeds, letting off the accelerator pedal requires vehicle deceleration dashpot airflow to cushion engine braking. Conversely, when the vehicle comes to a complete standstill, the engine controller must transition into true stationary idle speed regulation to maintain target idle RPM without causing vehicle creeping or engine surging. MPHREF establishes this vehicle speed boundary across multiple engine control routines, incorporating approximately 1.5 mph of built-in hysteresis to prevent rapid cycling around the switch point. In factory calibrations, MPHREF is set to 8 counts, corresponding to a vehicle speed threshold of 4.0 mph.

In factory calibrations, `MPHREF` is set to 8 counts, corresponding to a vehicle speed threshold of 4.0 mph.
MPHREF.tuners_guide: MPHREF controls the transition between rolling decel dashpot mode and stationary idle control. If your vehicle surges or hunts when creeping in heavy stop-and-go traffic or navigating tight parking lots at 3 to 5 mph, raising MPHREF to 6 or 8 mph (12 to 16 counts) forces the ECU into stationary idle control at slightly higher rolling speeds, stabilizing engine RPM while creeping. On manual transmission cars with lightweight flywheels, keeping MPHREF around 4 to 5 mph ensures that coasting to a stop sign keeps the dashpot active until the vehicle has almost completely stopped, preventing stall dips. Do not raise MPHREF above 10 mph, as stationary idle feedback will engage while coasting at road speeds, reducing engine vacuum braking.

* **Speed Threshold Limits**: * Avoid raising `MPHREF` above 10.0 mph to prevent unwanted idle hunting while coasting down hills.

PNDLTP.overview: PNDLTP defines the engine speed error threshold required before the controller triggers the automatic transmission Drive to Park/Neutral step reduction table. When the driver shifts an automatic transmission out of Drive or Reverse into Park or Neutral, the hydraulic load of the torque converter is suddenly released from the crankshaft. If the idle air stepper motor remained in its loaded in-gear position, the sudden uncoupling of transmission drag would cause the engine to flare upward loudly into a high-RPM surge. To prevent this flare, the ECU detects the RPM change upon shifting out of gear. If the difference between target idle speed and actual engine speed exceeds PNDLTP, the controller advances its memory pointer to index the DRPNK closing step table. In factory calibrations, PNDLTP is set to 160 counts, representing an RPM delta trigger threshold of approximately 80 RPM.

PNDLTP.tuners_guide: PNDLTP controls how sensitive the ECU is to shifting out of gear. PNDLT.overview: PNDLT defines the engine speed error deadband threshold required before the controller triggers the automatic transmission Park/Neutral to Drive kick opening table. When the driver shifts an automatic transmission from Park or Neutral into Drive or Reverse, the transmission hydraulic clutches engage and the torque converter impeller suddenly loads the crankshaft. To prevent the resulting mechanical drag from causing a severe engine stumble or stall, the ECU monitors the RPM drop. If the difference between actual engine speed and target idle speed exceeds PNDLT, the controller advances its memory pointer to index the PNDRK opening step table. In factory calibrations, PNDLT is configured to 400 counts, representing an RPM delta trigger threshold of approximately 200 RPM.

If the difference between actual engine speed and target idle speed exceeds `PNDLT`, the controller advances its memory pointer to index the `PNDRK` opening step table. In factory calibrations, `PNDLT` is configured to 400 counts, representing an RPM delta trigger threshold of approximately 200 RPM.
PNDLT.tuners_guide: PNDLT controls how quickly the ECU intervenes when shifting into gear. If shifting into Drive causes the engine RPM to sag deeply or die before the idle controller reacts, lowering PNDLT to 100 to 150 RPM (200 to 300 counts) makes the ECU trigger the PNDRK step kick at a smaller initial RPM drop, catching the engine earlier. However, if PNDLT is set too low (below 50 RPM), minor engine speed fluctuations in neutral can accidentally trigger the in-gear kick, causing unwanted idle flaring. For loose, high-stall aftermarket torque converters that produce very little idle drag, PNDLT can be raised to prevent premature step kicks.

* **Earlier In-Gear Catch**: * Lower `PNDLT` from 200 RPM down to 100 to 140 RPM to trigger the `PNDRK` kick sooner if the engine dips heavily when shifted into Drive.
* **High-Stall Torque Converters**: * High-stall converters generate less initial drag; `PNDLT` can be elevated to prevent unnecessary step kicks on gear selection.
* **Threshold Minimum**: * Do not lower `PNDLT` below 50 RPM to avoid false triggering from natural idle lope.

DRPNK.overview: DRPNK is a 2D calibration curve that establishes the closing step reduction applied to the idle air stepper motor when shifting an automatic transmission from Drive into Park or Neutral. While in gear, the idle air motor is held open further to overcome the hydraulic viscous drag of the torque converter. When the driver shifts into Park or Neutral, this converter load vanishes instantly. If the extra in-gear airflow were not removed immediately, the unloaded engine would flare to high RPM. DRPNK commands an instantaneous reduction in stepper motor opening steps as a function of engine coolant temperature. In factory calibrations, DRPNK commands a large step reduction during cold warm-up (approximately 15 to 20 steps) that tapers down to 6 to 8 steps when the engine is fully warmed up.

When the driver shifts into Park or Neutral, this converter load vanishes instantly. If the extra in-gear airflow were not removed immediately, the unloaded engine would flare to high RPM. DRPNK commands an instantaneous reduction in stepper motor opening steps as a function of engine coolant temperature. In factory calibrations, `DRPNK` commands a large step reduction during cold warm-up (approximately 15 to 20 steps) that tapers down to 6 to 8 steps when the engine is fully warmed up.
DRPNK.tuners_guide: DRPNK is the primary tuning curve for eliminating neutral flare upon gear selector release. If your engine revs up or flares loudly when shifting from Drive or Reverse into Park or Neutral, increasing the closing step magnitude in DRPNK will pull the idle air motor closed more aggressively, snuffing out the flare. However, if DRPNK values are increased too much, the motor will close too far, causing the engine speed to dip below target idle and stumble before recovering. Tune DRPNK so that shifting between Drive and Neutral produces an imperceptible transition where engine speed remains flat at target idle.
DRPNK.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Eliminating Park/Neutral Flare**: * Increase `DRPNK` step reduction by 3 to 6 steps if shifting out of gear produces a noticeable flare above 1200 RPM.
* **Preventing Shift Undershoot**: * If engine speed dives below target idle when shifting into Neutral, reduce `DRPNK` closing steps.
* **Seamless Gear Transitions**: * Properly balanced `DRPNK` and `PNDRK` curves produce completely flat, seamless gear shifts without RPM flaring or sagging.

PNDRK.overview: PNDRK is a 2D calibration curve that establishes the pre-emptive opening steps added to the idle air stepper motor when shifting an automatic transmission from Park or Neutral into Drive. When the transmission shifts into gear, the hydraulic torque converter immediately places a heavy mechanical drag on the crankshaft. If the engine controller relied purely on closed-loop feedback to catch this load, engine speed would sag significantly before the stepper motor could respond. PNDRK injects a rapid, pre-emptive kick opening into the stepper motor as a function of coolant temperature. PERKCK.overview: PERKCK defines the scaling percentage multiplier applied to the off-idle air conditioning airflow adder ACCTBL. AISMPH.overview: AISMPH defines the maximum vehicle speed ceiling for active rolling idle mode on manual transmission Chrysler vehicles. When coasting in neutral with the clutch disengaged, maintaining a slightly elevated rolling idle speed prevents the engine from stalling, provides vacuum assist for power brakes, and facilitates smooth rev-matching when shifting back into gear. However, above moderate driving speeds, the vehicle is coasting at highway velocity and should operate under normal deceleration dashpot rules rather than holding an elevated rolling idle target. AISMPH establishes this upper speed boundary. In factory calibrations, AISMPH is set to 0 counts (disabled in some automatic calibrations) or 16 counts (approximately 16 mph in manual variants), bounding rolling idle regulation to low-speed coasting.

RPMDLT.overview: RPMDLT defines the engine speed tolerance adder above target idle speed that permits entry into rolling idle mode on manual transmission vehicles. While coasting in neutral below the speed threshold set in AISMPH, the engine controller must decide whether engine speed is close enough to target idle to engage closed-loop rolling idle regulation. If actual engine speed is significantly higher than target idle (for instance, if the driver just downshifted or revved the engine), entering rolling idle mode prematurely would cause the controller to actively fight the descending revs. RPMDLT is added to target idle speed to form an upper RPM boundary. Only when actual engine speed is below this combined threshold is rolling idle mode activated. In factory calibrations, RPMDLT is set to 7 counts, corresponding to an RPM tolerance of approximately 56 RPM.

ISPDCY.overview: ISPDCY defines the RPM decrement step size subtracted from target idle speed during rolling idle decay. When a vehicle is operating in rolling idle mode, target idle speed is held at an elevated level. As the vehicle slows or steady rolling conditions continue, this elevated target speed must gently decay back down toward the baseline stationary idle target set in AISPN or AISCLD. ISPDCY sets the step reduction in target engine speed applied on each decay interval paced by DECAIS. In factory calibrations, ISPDCY is set to 4 counts, which decrements the target idle speed by approximately 32 RPM on each decay step until the base target is reached.

DECAIS.overview: DECAIS defines the loop counter bitmask that paces how frequently the target idle speed decay step ISPDCY is applied during rolling idle mode. To prevent abrupt steps in engine speed while rolling or coasting, the reduction of target idle speed must occur across a measured time interval. DECAIS masks the main program loop counter to enforce a deliberate delay between each decay step. In factory calibrations, DECAIS is set to 127 counts, representing a binary bitmask allowing one decay step every 128 main loop passes, or approximately every 1.4 seconds.

AISLMH.overview: AISLMH defines the upper step limit offset added to baseline idle position to clamp the maximum opening of the idle stepper motor during rolling idle mode. While operating in rolling idle mode, closed-loop feedback dynamically adjusts stepper motor position to match target rolling idle speed. In factory calibrations, AISLMH is set to 32 counts, capping rolling idle opening at 32 steps above baseline.
AISLMH.overview_markdown: `AISLMH` defines the upper step limit offset added to baseline idle position to clamp the maximum opening of the idle stepper motor during rolling idle mode. While operating in rolling idle mode, closed-loop feedback dynamically adjusts stepper motor position to match target rolling idle speed. If an unexpected load or manifold pressure transient occurs, or if the driver coasts downhill with the throttle closed, unconstrained closed-loop feedback could drive the stepper motor open to near-maximum travel, causing the engine to flare loudly upon clutching in. `AISLMH` establishes a protective upper boundary: the desired motor position during rolling idle is never permitted to exceed baseline steps plus `AISLMH`. In factory calibrations, `AISLMH` is set to 32 counts, capping rolling idle opening at 32 steps above baseline.
AISLMH.tuners_guide: AISLMH bounds the dynamic opening range of the idle stepper motor while rolling. If your vehicle exhibits an unwanted engine flare (such as revving up to 1800 or 2000 RPM) when coasting in neutral down slight hills, reducing AISLMH from 32 steps down to 15 to 20 steps restricts how far the stepper motor can open during rolling idle. Conversely, if rolling idle struggles to hold target speed when heavy loads turn on while coasting (such as electric cooling fans or headlights), increasing AISLMH to 40 to 45 steps provides additional opening headroom.
AISLMH.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Preventing Rolling Idle Flare**: * Lower `AISLMH` from 32 to 16 to 20 steps if engine speed flares upward while coasting in neutral.
* **Heavy Load Headroom**: * Increase `AISLMH` to 40 to 45 steps if large dual cooling fans pull down rolling idle speed below target.
* **Pairing with AISLML**: * Forms the upper boundary of the rolling idle window; balance against `AISLML` (lower floor).
AISLMH.operating_conditions:
Takes effect while operating in rolling idle mode, closed-loop feedback dynamically adjusts stepper motor position to match target rolling idle speed.

AISLML.overview: AISLML defines the lower step limit offset subtracted from baseline idle position to clamp the minimum opening of the idle stepper motor during rolling idle mode. While the vehicle is rolling in neutral with closed throttle, the engine relies on auxiliary bypass airflow to avoid sudden stalling when the brakes are applied or when clutching back into gear. If the closed-loop controller observed a minor overspeed and drove the stepper motor completely shut, the engine would be left with zero bypass air, causing an immediate stall when vehicle speed halted. AISLML establishes a protective lower floor: the desired motor position during rolling idle is never permitted to drop below baseline steps minus AISLML. In factory calibrations, AISLML is set to 4 counts, ensuring the stepper motor cannot close more than 4 steps below the calibrated baseline during rolling idle.

In factory calibrations, `AISLML` is set to 4 counts, ensuring the stepper motor cannot close more than 4 steps below the calibrated baseline during rolling idle.
AISLML.tuners_guide: AISLML protects against rolling idle undershoot stalls. If your engine dips below idle and stalls when you coast to a stop in neutral or apply the brakes while rolling, ensuring that AISLML is tightly bounded (between 2 and 4 steps) prevents the closed-loop controller from over-retracting the stepper motor. If you have an aggressive camshaft that needs a high, steady baseline airflow while rolling, reducing AISLML to 2 steps (or even 0 steps) keeps the stepper motor firmly propped at or above the baseline position. Never increase AISLML above 10 steps, as this allows the motor to step down too far, risking a decel die-out.
AISLML.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Coasting Undershoot Protection**: * Keep `AISLML` between 2 and 4 steps to guarantee that the idle stepper motor cannot choke off bypass air while rolling to a stop.
* **Aggressive Camshaft Floor**: * Lower `AISLML` to 1 or 2 steps on high-overlap camshafts to ensure rolling idle never drops below the baseline airflow floor.
* **Excessive Travel Warning**: * Avoid setting `AISLML` higher than 8 steps, as the controller can pull the motor shut on rolling overspeeds, inducing stalls.

BTVAIS.overview: BTVAIS defines the minimum electrical system battery voltage required before the controller allows actuation of the automatic idle speed stepper motor. The 4-wire stepper motor actuator relies on electromagnetic coils to overcome internal friction, spring pressure, and intake manifold vacuum force to move the pintle. If battery voltage sags significantly, coil current is insufficient to overcome these mechanical forces, leading to weak torque, skipped steps, and permanent loss of motor position calibration. BTVAIS establishes a protective voltage floor: whenever battery voltage is below BTVAIS, stepper motor stepping pulses are completely inhibited. In factory calibrations, BTVAIS is set to 113 counts, corresponding to a battery voltage floor of approximately 11.3 Volts.

The 4-wire stepper motor actuator relies on electromagnetic coils to overcome internal friction, spring pressure, and intake manifold vacuum force to move the pintle. If battery voltage sags significantly, coil current is insufficient to overcome these mechanical forces, leading to weak torque, skipped steps, and permanent loss of motor position calibration. `BTVAIS` establishes a protective voltage floor: whenever battery voltage is below `BTVAIS`, stepper motor stepping pulses are completely inhibited. In factory calibrations, `BTVAIS` is set to 113 counts, corresponding to a battery voltage floor of approximately 11.3 Volts.
BTVAIS.tuners_guide: BTVAIS protects the idle air stepper motor from losing calibration during severe electrical system load transients. If running a lightweight racing battery or a high-draw aftermarket audio or fuel pump system that causes system voltage to dip momentarily to 11.0 Volts during hot idle, the factory 11.3 Volt threshold may temporarily freeze idle air motor corrections. In such cases, lowering BTVAIS slightly to 10.5 or 10.8 Volts (105 to 108 counts) maintains idle air control authority during heavy electrical draw. Never lower BTVAIS below 9.5 Volts, as stepper motor coils will reliably skip steps under manifold vacuum when supplied with inadequate voltage.
BTVAIS.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Lightweight Battery Dip Accommodation**: * Lower `BTVAIS` to 10.5 to 10.8 Volts if high-draw electric water pumps or fuel pumps pull system voltage below 11.3 Volts at hot idle.
* **Skipped Step Hazard**: * Do not lower `BTVAIS` below 9.5 Volts, as weak coil magnetism at low voltage causes the stepper motor to miscount steps and lose physical calibration.
* **Factory Safety Margin**: * Factory setting of 113 counts (11.3 Volts) ensures robust coil stepping torque under all factory operating conditions.
BTVAIS.operating_conditions:
Takes effect if battery voltage sags significantly, coil current is insufficient to overcome these mechanical forces, leading to weak torque, skipped steps, and permanent loss of motor position calibration.

AISHLM.overview: AISHLM establishes the absolute high limit clamp for the maximum number of open steps that can ever be commanded on the automatic idle speed stepper motor. The Chrysler 4-wire stepper motor actuator physically drives a tapered pintle in and out of an auxiliary throttle bypass passage. If the controller were to continuously increment stepper opening steps without an upper limit, the motor mechanism could unscrew the pintle shaft from its internal worm gear drive or jam the actuator against its mechanical end stops, causing lost steps and permanent positioning calibration errors. Furthermore, beyond approximately 160 steps, the annular bypass opening around the pintle is completely unrestricted, and additional opening steps provide zero incremental airflow. In factory calibrations, AISHLM is configured to 160 counts, locking maximum stepper opening at exactly 160 steps across all idle, startup, decel, and air conditioning routines.

The Chrysler 4-wire stepper motor actuator physically drives a tapered pintle in and out of an auxiliary throttle bypass passage. If the controller were to continuously increment stepper opening steps without an upper limit, the motor mechanism could unscrew the pintle shaft from its internal worm gear drive or jam the actuator against its mechanical end stops, causing lost steps and permanent positioning calibration errors. Furthermore, beyond approximately 160 steps, the annular bypass opening around the pintle is completely unrestricted, and additional opening steps provide zero incremental airflow. In factory calibrations, `AISHLM` is configured to 160 counts, locking maximum stepper opening at exactly 160 steps across all idle, startup, decel, and air conditioning routines.
AISHLM.tuners_guide: AISHLM should generally remain at 160 steps for factory and stock-style throttle bodies. Raising AISHLM above 160 steps does not provide additional airflow on stock Chrysler throttle bodies because the bypass port reaches complete aerodynamic saturation at approximately 150 to 160 steps. However, if installing an aftermarket custom throttle body or high-flow remote idle air control housing with an extended pintle stroke and larger bore, AISHLM can be increased up to 180 or 200 steps to utilize the extended mechanical travel. Never set AISHLM above 240 steps, as this risks driving the stepper motor pintle completely off its internal drive threads, resulting in a physically jammed idle air valve.
AISHLM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Stock Throttle Body Saturation**: * Keep `AISHLM` at 160 steps on factory throttle bodies; the bypass passage is fully open by 150 steps and additional travel yields zero extra air.
* **Extended-Stroke Aftermarket Housings**: * For custom high-flow idle air valve housings designed for extended travel, `AISHLM` can be safely raised to 180 to 200 steps.
* **Mechanical Disassembly Hazard**: * Setting `AISHLM` above 240 steps can cause the stepper motor screw to unthread or bind against physical stops, causing total idle control failure.
AISHLM.operating_conditions:
Takes effect whenever the idle air motor steps open, enforcing an absolute upper mechanical limit on stepper pintle travel to prevent motor jamming.

CALPOS.overview: CALPOS defines the calibrated nominal step position where the electronic controller assumes the idle air stepper motor sits during normal warm closed-throttle idle. Because stepper motors operate without a physical position feedback potentiometer, the ECU tracks motor position by counting step pulses sent to the motor coils. During closed-throttle stationary idle, adaptive routines periodically nudge motor position toward CALPOS to maintain optimal dynamic control range. Additionally, CALPOS serves as the fundamental baseline offset added to startup positioning curves and cold idle tables. In factory calibrations, CALPOS is set to 26 counts, representing 26 open steps from the fully seated pintle position on a stock throttle body.
CALPOS.overview_markdown: `CALPOS` defines the calibrated nominal step position where the electronic controller assumes the idle air stepper motor sits during normal warm closed-throttle idle. Because stepper motors operate without a physical position feedback potentiometer, the ECU tracks motor position by counting step pulses sent to the motor coils. During closed-throttle stationary idle, adaptive routines periodically nudge motor position toward `CALPOS` to maintain optimal dynamic control range. Additionally, `CALPOS` serves as the fundamental baseline offset added to startup positioning curves and cold idle tables. In factory calibrations, `CALPOS` is set to 26 counts, representing 26 open steps from the fully seated pintle position on a stock throttle body.
CALPOS.tuners_guide: CALPOS must be adjusted whenever the mechanical throttle body is modified or replaced. If an aftermarket 52mm or 58mm throttle body is installed, or if the mechanical minimum air stop screw is turned inward to admit more bypass air for an aggressive camshaft, the engine will require fewer stepper motor steps to idle at target RPM. If CALPOS remains at 26 steps while the engine only needs 10 steps to idle, the adaptive routines will constantly fight to pull the motor closed. Monitor live datalogging of idle steps on a fully warmed engine; if the motor sits at 12 steps, set CALPOS to 12. Setting CALPOS to reflect true warmed-up idle steps ensures maximum dynamic opening authority during sudden load changes.
CALPOS.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Aftermarket Throttle Bodies**: * Big-bore throttle bodies allow more air leakage; adjust `CALPOS` down to 10 to 18 steps to match the lower step counts observed in live datalogs.
* **Mechanical Stop Screw Adjustment**: * If you turn the base idle stop screw inward to provide more base air for a race camshaft, reduce `CALPOS` correspondingly to keep adaptive trim centered.
* **Centering Adaptive Trim**: * Setting `CALPOS` accurately gives the idle stepper motor equal dynamic range to step open or closed when loads change.
CALPOS.operating_conditions:
Takes effect during closed-throttle stationary idle, adaptive routines periodically nudge motor position toward CALPOS to maintain optimal dynamic control range.

CALRAT.overview: CALRAT defines the loop counter bitmask that paces how frequently the engine controller nudges the automatic idle speed stepper motor toward its nominal idle position. When the engine is idling at steady state with engine speed within a narrow window around target idle, the ECU gradually converges the stepper motor toward the calibrated baseline step position set in CALPOS. To prevent this centering action from causing perceptible idle speed fluctuations or fighting closed-loop proportional corrections, updates must occur very slowly. CALRAT masks the main program loop counter to enforce a deliberate update interval. In factory calibrations, CALRAT is configured to 7 counts, which functions as a binary bitmask allowing an adjustment only once every 8 main loop cycles, or approximately every 88 milliseconds.

When the engine is idling at steady state with engine speed within a narrow window around target idle, the ECU gradually converges the stepper motor toward the calibrated baseline step position set in `CALPOS`. To prevent this centering action from causing perceptible idle speed fluctuations or fighting closed-loop proportional corrections, updates must occur very slowly. `CALRAT` masks the main program loop counter to enforce a deliberate update interval. In factory calibrations, `CALRAT` is configured to 7 counts, which functions as a binary bitmask allowing an adjustment only once every 8 main loop cycles, or approximately every 88 milliseconds.
CALRAT.tuners_guide: CALRAT rarely needs modification unless you are debugging idle hunting issues on custom induction setups. If the engine hunts or wanders slowly around target idle because the background centering logic is pulling the stepper motor too aggressively toward CALPOS, increasing CALRAT to 15 (every 16th loop) or 31 (every 32nd loop) slows down the centering rate. Lowering CALRAT to 3 (every 4th loop) speeds up convergence toward CALPOS, but doing so risks inducing an artificial surge if CALPOS does not perfectly match the engine's true mechanical idle airflow requirement.
CALRAT.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Pacing Centering Action**: * Keep `CALRAT` at 7 counts for factory-like convergence pacing toward `CALPOS`.
* **Slowing Adaptive Wander**: * On engines with aftermarket camshafts where idle airflow requirements drift slightly with engine temperature, raise `CALRAT` to 15 or 31 counts to slow down background position nudging.
* **Surge Hazard**: * Do not set `CALRAT` to 0 or 1, as rapid position nudging will conflict directly with the `FWDAIS`/`REVAIS` feedback loops.

Takes effect when the engine is idling at steady state with engine speed within a narrow window around target idle, the ECU gradually converges the stepper motor toward the calibrated baseline step position set in CALPOS.

MAPHI.overview: MAPHI (HiMAP3DInputModifierFromMAP) defines the axis coordinate transfer function and breakpoint scaling curve for Manifold Pressure (MAP) used by the ECU's 3D table interpolation routines. T92F5X.overview: T92F5X represents unassigned ROM alignment padding bytes ($FF) allocated within the calibration structure. In Chrysler MPTune calibration templates, Type 9 padding tables are inserted to fill unused memory gaps between active calibration tables, ensuring that subsequent tables align with fixed 16-byte or 256-byte binary address boundaries. These bytes are static ROM filler and are never loaded, evaluated, or executed by the 68HC11 engine controller firmware.

SRCID.overview: SRCID defines the Turbonator custom codebase version and controller family identifier within the calibration header. In custom firmware, SRCID replaces unused factory plant testing codes to provide positive identification of the underlying firmware architecture. Encoded as a sixteen-bit word, the upper byte designates the engine controller architecture (such as zero B for the SBEC-II family, zero A for SBEC-IIs, and zero C for SBEC controllers), while the lower byte indicates the firmware version in hexadecimal (such as nineteen in hexadecimal to designate version nineteen). Tuning editors query SRCID to automatically verify table compatibility and unlock platform-specific features.
SRCID.overview_markdown: `SRCID` defines the Turbonator custom codebase version and controller family identifier within the calibration header. In custom firmware, `SRCID` replaces unused factory plant testing codes to provide positive identification of the underlying firmware architecture. Encoded as a sixteen-bit word, the upper byte designates the engine controller architecture (such as zero B for the SBEC-II family, zero A for SBEC-IIs, and zero C for SBEC controllers), while the lower byte indicates the firmware version in hexadecimal (such as nineteen in hexadecimal to designate version nineteen). Tuning editors query `SRCID` to automatically verify table compatibility and unlock platform-specific features.
SRCID.tuners_guide: Tuners should leave SRCID matched to the exact firmware codebase loaded into the controller. MPTune and other calibration editors use SRCID to detect which custom features are available, such as switchable boost, two-step launch control, anti-lag timing retards, and wideband oxygen sensor conversion. If SRCID is modified incorrectly, calibration software may load incorrect table definitions or hide advanced tuning controls. In addition, changing SRCID modifies the memory checksum, requiring a corresponding fixup in the checksum constant.
SRCID.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Codebase & Version Tracking**: * Identifies the ECU platform (T-SBECII) and firmware release (Version 19) to tuning software.
* **Feature Compatibility**: * Tuning suites like MPTune query `SRCID` to enable version-specific features (launch control, 3-bar scaling, anti-lag).
* **Firmware Anomaly**: * Not executed by any CPU instructions in `T-SBECII_v19.asm`; functions strictly as a calibration metadata tag and checksum contributor.

TMPTL1.overview: TMPTL1 is the primary non-linear transfer table converting raw voltage counts from the engine coolant temperature sensor into engineering temperature units under cold operating conditions. The Chrysler SBEC-II hardware incorporates a dual-range thermistor input circuit with a switched pull-up resistor. When the engine is cold (ranging from minus forty degrees Fahrenheit up to approximately one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit), the controller switches the circuit to high sensitivity and looks up coolant temperature through this seven-point curve. By expanding sensor resolution across low temperatures, TMPTL1 provides precise cold-start fueling enrichment, cranking fuel scheduling, and cold idle target control.

When the engine is cold (ranging from minus forty degrees Fahrenheit up to approximately one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit), the controller switches the circuit to high sensitivity and looks up coolant temperature through this seven-point curve. By expanding sensor resolution across low temperatures, `TMPTL1` provides precise cold-start fueling enrichment, cranking fuel scheduling, and cold idle target control.
TMPTL1.tuners_guide: TMPTL1 is calibrated to match the resistance characteristics of the factory Chrysler negative temperature coefficient coolant thermistor. Tuners rarely need to modify this table unless retrofitting an aftermarket or non-Chrysler engine coolant temperature sensor with a different resistance curve. If an aftermarket sensor is installed, recalibrating TMPTL1 is necessary to ensure accurate cold-start fueling, proper warmup enrichment decay, and reliable cold-weather starting.
TMPTL1.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Factory Thermistor Match**: * Matches the low-temperature resistance curve of the factory Chrysler two-pin coolant temperature sensor.
* **Aftermarket Sensor Swaps**: * If swapping to a non-stock sensor (such as a GM or Bosch thermistor), `TMPTL1` must be re-curved to maintain cold-start enrichment accuracy.
* **Cold-Range Resolution**: * Dedicated to engine temperatures below one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit, where fuel vaporization is minimal.
* **Companion Curve**: * Seamlessly hands off to `TMPTL2` as the engine reaches normal operating temperature.

TMPTL2.overview: TMPTL2 is the hot-range non-linear transfer table converting raw voltage counts from the engine coolant temperature sensor into engineering temperature units under warm running conditions. When coolant temperature warms past approximately one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit, the controller hardware toggles the thermistor pull-up resistor to its low-resistance mode and the firmware switches lookup from the cold scale to this four-point hot scale curve. Because all normal operating temperatures (one hundred eighty to two hundred ten degrees Fahrenheit) reside on TMPTL2, this table directly governs radiator fan cycling, closed-loop fuel trim engagement, adaptive purge flow, and warmup spark modifiers.

* **Hysteresis Switching**: * Toggles between `TMPTL1` and `TMPTL2` with built-in voltage deadband filtering to prevent hunting at 140 degF.

DWELL.overview: DWELL defines the primary ignition coil dwell time curve indexed by battery voltage. Ignition coil dwell represents the duration in microseconds that the ignition driver transistor grounds the coil primary winding, allowing electrical current and magnetic flux to saturate the coil core before opening the circuit to fire the spark plug. Battery voltage is the primary physical factor governing coil saturation: at low battery voltages (such as during cold cranking or charging system faults, between 8 and 10 Volts), current builds slowly through the coil windings, requiring extended dwell times (up to 8.2 milliseconds). At normal vehicle operating voltages (13.5 to 14.5 Volts), the coil charges much faster, requiring only 2.2 to 2.5 milliseconds. The calibration table stores the mathematical one's complement of the dwell period because the controller's 16-bit table interpolation routine requires an upward-sloping curve.

Ignition coil dwell represents the duration in microseconds that the ignition driver transistor grounds the coil primary winding, allowing electrical current and magnetic flux to saturate the coil core before opening the circuit to fire the spark plug. Battery voltage is the primary physical factor governing coil saturation: at low battery voltages (such as during cold cranking or charging system faults, between 8 and 10 Volts), current builds slowly through the coil windings, requiring extended dwell times (up to 8.2 milliseconds). At normal vehicle operating voltages (13.5 to 14.5 Volts), the coil charges much faster, requiring only 2.2 to 2.5 milliseconds. The calibration table stores the mathematical one's complement of the dwell period because the controller's 16-bit table interpolation routine requires an upward-sloping curve.
DWELL.tuners_guide: Adjusting DWELL is necessary when upgrading from the factory ignition coil to aftermarket high-energy coils, multi-spark systems, or modern low-inductance coils that feature different primary resistance and charge saturation curves. Increasing dwell times provides greater magnetic saturation and hotter spark energy, which can help prevent spark blowout under high boost and dense cylinder charges. However, commanding excessive dwell causes severe internal coil heating, premature ignition coil failure, and electrical stress on the ECU's internal power switching transistor. Insufficient dwell results in weak spark energy, leading to high-load misfires or spark blowout as boost levels rise.
DWELL.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Aftermarket Coil Matching**: * High-performance aftermarket coils (such as MSD Blaster or Accel coils) typically have lower primary resistance; consult coil manufacturer specifications to avoid over-saturating the primary winding.
* **Preventing Spark Blowout**: * On high-boost applications (20+ psi), slightly increasing dwell at 13 to 14 Volts ensures full coil saturation to jump large spark plug gaps under dense cylinder pressures.
* **Coil Overheating Caution**: * Never set dwell beyond coil saturation; excessive dwell dissipates purely as heat inside the coil casing and power transistor.
* **One's Complement Encoding**: * Stored in ROM as the one's complement; MPTune handles the inversion automatically so the tuner views true microseconds.

BTLRPM.overview: BTLRPM defines the minimum engine speed threshold required before the engine controller evaluates low-voltage charging system performance. Automotive alternators produce limited electrical current at low engine idle speeds, and high electrical accessory loads such as headlights, heater blower fans, and radiator cooling fans can easily exceed alternator capacity at idle, causing battery voltage to dip temporarily. To prevent nuisance fault codes during prolonged idling, the engine controller suppresses low-voltage alternator fault checking whenever engine speed is below BTLRPM. In factory calibrations, BTLRPM is set to 46 counts, corresponding to approximately 1472 RPM. If engine speed is at or above BTLRPM and battery voltage remains more than 1.0 volt below target charging voltage, the controller flags Fault Code 41.
BTLRPM.overview_markdown: `BTLRPM` defines the minimum engine speed threshold required before the engine controller evaluates low-voltage charging system performance. Automotive alternators produce limited electrical current at low engine idle speeds, and high electrical accessory loads such as headlights, heater blower fans, and radiator cooling fans can easily exceed alternator capacity at idle, causing battery voltage to dip temporarily. To prevent nuisance fault codes during prolonged idling, the engine controller suppresses low-voltage alternator fault checking whenever engine speed is below `BTLRPM`. In factory calibrations, `BTLRPM` is set to 46 counts, corresponding to approximately 1472 RPM. If engine speed is at or above `BTLRPM` and battery voltage remains more than 1.0 volt below target charging voltage, the controller flags **Fault Code 41**.
BTLRPM.tuners_guide: BTLRPM controls the engine speed gate that prevents false charging system error codes at stoplights and idle. On vehicles modified with underdrive crankshaft pulleys, high-amp electric cooling fans, or heavy aftermarket audio systems, alternator rotor speed is reduced and electrical demand is elevated at idle, causing battery voltage to sag frequently. Raising BTLRPM to 1600 or 1700 RPM prevents nuisance Fault Code 41 triggers during low-speed driving. Lowering BTLRPM enables low-voltage fault detection closer to idle, but increases the likelihood of false alternator codes when heavy electrical loads cycle on at idle. Zeroing BTLRPM causes the engine controller to evaluate charging voltage at idle, frequently flagging Fault Code 41 whenever the radiator cooling fan engages.
BTLRPM.tuners_guide_markdown:
* **Underdrive Pulleys & Electrical Accessories**: * Underdrive pulleys spin the alternator slower at idle, reducing current output. * Raise `BTLRPM` from 1472 RPM to 1600-1700 RPM to suppress false Fault Code 41 errors on modified pulley setups.
* **Diagnostic Sensitivity**: * Lowering `BTLRPM` tests charging performance at lower engine speeds, but risks false fault logging during heavy electrical draw at idle.
* **Edge Cases**: * Setting `BTLRPM` to zero triggers Fault Code 41 during normal idle with headlights and heater fan on. * Setting `BTLRPM` to maximum (e.g., 6000 RPM) disables low-voltage alternator fault monitoring entirely.
